processing: Made like other Wuyi rock teas: oxidised, twisted into strips and roasted. Roast varies by maker.
harvest_season: Spring, as with other Wuyi rock teas.
appearance_dry: Dark, twisted strips, as with other Rou Gui.
appearance_wet: Dark leaves with reddened edges, typical of Wuyi Rou Gui.
taste_profile: Rou Gui's cinnamon spice with a strong mineral rock character, as the area is known for; given the fakes, your cup may vary widely.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, short steeps. If you do have a genuine lot, do not waste it on a long first steep.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year, usually after roasting and rest, at prices among the highest in Wuyi. Reported supply from the core area is tiny compared with what is on sale, so most tea with this name cannot be from there. Buy from a maker you trust.
description:
Niu Lan Keng, Cow Pen Gully, is one of the three gullies and two streams, the classic core of Wuyi rock tea. Rou Gui from here is nicknamed Niu Rou, beef, and is the most hyped tea in the region.

The making is ordinary rock tea craft and the plant is ordinary Rou Gui. The whole premium rests on the place, whose rock character is held to be among the strongest in the area.

The cup should show cinnamon spice with a dense mineral finish. Use boiling water and short steeps.

Fakes are the main issue. Press investigations put the core area at only twenty to thirty mu and output at some 500 kg, and yet online listings run to at least a hundred products, while the area claimed has been stretched with invented sub-sections. Even veteran makers say they cannot identify the place by taste alone.

If the price seems low, it is almost certainly from elsewhere. A well-made Rou Gui with an honest label is the better purchase.
history:
Niu Lan Keng is long listed among Wuyi's three gullies and two streams. Its fame as a Rou Gui name is much more recent, and the Niu Rou nickname is trade language.

The hype drew press scrutiny of pricing and false origin claims. Wuyishan has been working on origin tracing and a census of tea gardens in response.
